concepts.title: Totipotency and the History of Plant Tissue Culture

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Totipotency and the History of Plant Tissue Culture' refers to.
questions.a: Every living plant cell keeps the totipotent power to regenerate a whole plant, the intuition Haberlandt advanced in 1902 that earned him the fatherhood of the field; kinetin arrived in 1955, the Skoog-Miller 1957 ratio rule tied organ fate to hormone balance, Murashige and Skoog's 1962 salt-rich medium became the standard, and Guha and Maheshwari's 1964 anther-culture haploids opened the door to somatic hybrids, Pomato of 1978 and the somaclonal variation named in 1981.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Totipotency and the History of Plant Tissue Culture'.
questions.a: One vegetative cell can rebuild the entire plant - the promise that turned tissue culture into both a science and an industry.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Totipotency and the History of Plant Tissue Culture' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 7.1 (source: lebt107.txt section 7.1, Box 1)

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Explant Preparation and Culture Steps' refers to.
questions.a: Culturing starts with an explant - meristem, leaf, cotyledon, hypocotyl or embryo - surface-sterilised in sodium hypochlorite, rinsed and inoculated onto sterile medium; the tissue then dedifferentiates into callus, redifferentiates organ primordia through organogenesis or follows somatic embryogenesis, with regenerated shoots rooted and plantlets hardened toward the field, immature embryos responding best among explant choices.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Explant Preparation and Culture Steps'.
questions.a: Sterilise, inoculate, dedifferentiate, redifferentiate, root and harden - the pipeline from explant to field-ready plantlet.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Explant Preparation and Culture Steps' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 7.2 (source: lebt107.txt section 7.2, Fig. 7.1)

concepts.title: Auxin Cytokinin Balance in Nutrient Media

questions.q: Using the method 'Auxin Cytokinin Balance in Nutrient Media', work with: auxin_level = 400, kinetin_level = 240. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of excess.
questions.a: 160 units

questions.q: Take the relation taught for 'Auxin Cytokinin Balance in Nutrient Media' and work with: auxin_level = 25, kinetin_level = 15. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of excess.
questions.a: 10 units

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Auxin Cytokinin Balance in Nutrient Media' refers to.
questions.a: Media blend macronutrients, micronutrients, amino acids, B vitamins, two to five percent sucrose, gelling agar, optional antibiotics and minute doses of five hormone classes; the auxin-cytokinin ratio rules morphogenesis - excess auxin roots, excess cytokinin shoots, and intermediate balance proliferates callus - while a pH set around 5.8-6.0 keeps the gel firm and the salts soluble.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Auxin Cytokinin Balance in Nutrient Media'.
questions.a: Divide auxin by cytokinin - a quotient above one pushes roots, below one pushes shoots, near one keeps callus.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Auxin Cytokinin Balance in Nutrient Media', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: hormone_ratio = auxin_level / kinetin_level

concepts.title: MS Medium Strength versus White Medium

questions.q: Using the method 'MS Medium Strength versus White Medium', work with: ms_conc = 240, white_conc = 40. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of extra_mg.
questions.a: 200 units

questions.q: Take the relation taught for 'MS Medium Strength versus White Medium' and work with: ms_conc = 100, white_conc = 30. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of extra_mg.
questions.a: 70 units

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'MS Medium Strength versus White Medium' refers to.
questions.a: Murashige and Skoog's formulation is a salt powerhouse next to White's classic recipe: potassium nitrate runs 1900 against 80 milligrams per litre and ammonium nitrate adds 1650 where White has none, thiamine sits at 0.5 rather than 0.01, and sucrose rises from 20 to 30 grams per litre - richness that lets MS culture a far wider range of species.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'MS Medium Strength versus White Medium'.
questions.a: Divide each MS concentration by its White's value to see how much stronger the modern medium is.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'MS Medium Strength versus White Medium', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: ms_fold = ms_conc / white_conc

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Micropropagation and Synthetic Seeds' refers to.
questions.a: Micropropagation clones elite, rare or non-fertile plants season-free in flasks - India alone regenerates over 400 million banana plantlets a year - while synthetic seeds encapsulate somatic embryos in calcium alginate coats loaded with nutrients and regulators, storing and shipping clonal stock of carrot, grape or sandalwood without any seed at all.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Micropropagation and Synthetic Seeds'.
questions.a: Multiply one elite genotype into millions, then pack the embryos in alginate beads that behave like true seeds.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Micropropagation and Synthetic Seeds' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 7.5 (source: lebt107.txt section 7.5, Fig. 7.3)

concepts.title: Haploids Double Haploids and Somatic Hybrids

questions.q: Using the method 'Haploids Double Haploids and Somatic Hybrids', work with: haploid_count = 500. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of homozygous_pairs.
questions.a: 500 units

questions.q: Take the relation taught for 'Haploids Double Haploids and Somatic Hybrids' and work with: haploid_count = 5. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of homozygous_pairs.
questions.a: 5 units

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Haploids Double Haploids and Somatic Hybrids' refers to.
questions.a: Anther, pollen or ovary culture yields haploids whose colchicine doubling produces homozygous diploids that expose recessive traits for breeders; protoplasts stripped by cellulase and pectinase fuse under polyethylene glycol across species barriers - Carlson's 1972 Nicotiana hybrids began the era, Pomato mixed potato with tomato, and cybridisation even pairs one parent's nucleus with another's mitochondria or chloroplasts.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Haploids Double Haploids and Somatic Hybrids'.
questions.a: Double the haploid chromosome set with colchicine and the clone turns homozygous diploid; fuse protoplasts and species barriers fall.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Haploids Double Haploids and Somatic Hybrids', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: doubled_count = haploid_count * 2

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Meristem Culture for Virus-Free Plants' refers to.
questions.a: Viruses scatter unevenly through plant bodies and leave the apical and axillary meristems clean, so excising a meristem tip shorter than one millimetre and culturing it regenerates sugarcane, banana or potato stock entirely free of virus - rescuing yields in clonally propagated crops where every infected cutting infects its whole lineage.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Meristem Culture for Virus-Free Plants'.
questions.a: Take the tiniest meristem - under a millimetre - where no virus has reached, and grow a clean clone from it.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Meristem Culture for Virus-Free Plants' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 7.5 (source: lebt107.txt section 7.5 (Production of virus-free plants))

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Somaclonal Variation and Secondary Metabolites' refers to.
questions.a: Culture both creates and harvests plant chemistry: somaclonal variations - the term Larkin and Scowcroft coined in 1981 - pass somatic mutations into regenerated plants, a bane for clonal fidelity but a boon yielding disease-resistant sugarcane, banana and tomato cultivars; meanwhile cell suspensions and hairy roots overproduce secondary metabolites from artemisinin and azadirachtin to taxol, shikonin and vincristine, independent of season and without stripping wild populations.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Somaclonal Variation and Secondary Metabolites'.
questions.a: Culture-induced variants can be screened as new cultivars, and cultured cells can out-produce the whole plant in valuable metabolites.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Somaclonal Variation and Secondary Metabolites' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 7.5 (source: lebt107.txt section 7.5, Box 3)
